scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originates from the Miyako Islands in the Ryukyu archipelago.
Its name, derived from 'kui' (voice) and 'chaasu' (to combine), reflects its roots as a communal vocal tradition.
It gained significant historical weight in the early 20th century as a medium to celebrate the abolition of the Nintōzei poll tax in 1903.
on_screen: Map: Japan · East Asia
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It is performed for harvest festivals (Hōnen) and historical commemorations.
It serves as a prayer for the 'year of Miroku' (a golden age) and as a celebration of freedom from historical taxation and forced labor.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form a circle and engage in a vigorous, rhythmic performance.
Key movements include shaking arms to and fro and side to side, stamping legs forcefully on the ground, jumping high, and clapping hands in sync with the group singing.
Watch for Stamping, Arm Shaking.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Kuichaa is characterized by group singing (kuichaa-aagu) with free verse forms.
It is primarily vocal and percussive, using hand claps and foot stamps for rhythm.
Listen for the Voice, Hand claps.

A powerful blend of unison group singing and percussive body sounds. The music is driven by the 'kui' (combined voices) of the participants, punctuated by sharp hand claps and the heavy, resonant thud of feet stamping in unison on the earth.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Traditionally performed in outdoor communal spaces such as village squares or ports.
While specific costumes are not detailed in the primary source, the dance is historically linked to the working clothes of Miyako farmers and weavers.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Scholar Hokama Shuzen is noted for his etymological research into the dance.
The 'representatives of farmers' who ended the poll tax are the central historical figures celebrated in the lyrics.
Variants include the 'Parumizu nu kuichaa' (commemorating tax abolition) and 'Hōnen no Kuichaa' (harvest prayer).
Kuichaa is a subclass of Ryukyuan group dance and is closely related to the 'aagu' epic song tradition of the Miyako Islands.
